name: Somapacitan
lead: Somapacitan (brand name Sogroya, development name NNC0195-0092) is a once-weekly growth hormone (GH) derivative made by Novo Nordisk, given by subcutaneous injection [1][2][16]. It is used to support growth in children with diagnosed growth hormone deficiency and certain short-stature conditions, and to replace GH in adults with deficiency, where GH influences body composition, including fat distribution and lean mass [12][20]. Its appeal for appearance-related goals in communities such as looksmax.org is the possibility of added height, and the published research on that question is confined to children with diagnosed growth conditions whose growth plates are still open.

The molecule is a human GH analog with a small attached albumin-binding group. Binding to albumin is reversible and slows the drug's elimination, which allows weekly rather than daily dosing [16][19]. The US label covers children aged 2.5 years and older with GH deficiency, short stature after being born small for gestational age without catch-up growth, Noonan syndrome growth failure and idiopathic short stature, as well as adults with GH deficiency [12].

Phase 3 trials examined it in children (REAL 4) and adults (REAL 1), and long-term follow-up of the phase 2 REAL 3 trial has reached four years [1][2][6][9]. In pediatric GH deficiency, reviews describe height velocity similar to daily GH and a comparable safety profile across the long-acting class [7][18]. It is a prescription medicine; one looksmax.org thread asks whether it is worth using and where pediatric growth hormone products can be found, without substantive reply [11].

paras: Somapacitan is prescribed as a growth hormone replacement. In children, the goal is to raise growth rate (height velocity) toward the normal range; in adults, the goal is to restore GH activity, which affects fat mass, lean mass and metabolic markers [12][20].

For pediatric patients aged 2.5 years and older, the US label lists growth failure due to inadequate GH secretion, short stature in children born small for gestational age who have not caught up by age 2, growth failure associated with Noonan syndrome, and idiopathic short stature [12]. Growth hormone therapy works while the growth plates (epiphyses) remain open, and the pediatric trials enrolled prepubertal children [1][4][5]. Whether weekly dosing changes the final adult height compared with daily dosing is being followed in extension studies and long-term surveillance registries [13][15][24].

Wikipedia reports that in Eli Lilly's late-1990s Humatrope trials in short but otherwise typical children, adult height gain after about four years of daily GH was roughly 4 to 8 cm, and that in Turner syndrome median adult height gain was about 5 to 8 cm [17]. These figures concern daily GH products, not somapacitan; adult-height data for weekly products are still accumulating [13][15][24].

In adults with GH deficiency, GH replacement is used to address increased truncal fat and reduced lean mass. A clinicians' guide to adult use summarises trial data showing decreased truncal fat, improved visceral fat and lean body mass and neutral effects on glucose metabolism [20].

Somapacitan is produced by recombinant DNA technology in E. coli and differs from natural GH by an attached non-covalent albumin-binding moiety [16]. The long-acting class aims to reduce the burden of daily injections and improve adherence [19][21].

According to the label, somapacitan binds a dimeric GH receptor on target cells, with some effects mediated by IGF-1 produced in the liver and others direct [12]. Reversible binding to albumin acts as a reservoir that lengthens the time the drug stays in circulation [16][19]. Because IGF-1 reflects GH exposure, a study examined how best to time and interpret IGF-1 measurements during once-weekly therapy [10].

Early work characterised the drug in healthy subjects, children and adults, including a first-in-human trial and studies in people with kidney or liver impairment and a mass-balance study [15][25][26][27]. A modelling analysis of three phase 1 trials supported the dosing rationale for children and adults [28].

Wikipedia gives somapacitan a molar mass of about 23,305 g/mol and describes it as made in E. coli, with a small albumin-binding group attached to a human GH analog [16]. The US label uses the suffix form somapacitan-beco [12][16].

The US label lists warnings including increased mortality in acute critical illness, severe hypersensitivity, increased risk of neoplasms (notably second neoplasms in childhood cancer survivors treated with radiation to the head), glucose intolerance and diabetes mellitus, intracranial hypertension, fluid retention, hypoadrenalism and hypothyroidism [12]. Label pregnancy information notes no human data for somapacitan, that published studies of short-acting recombinant GH have not identified a drug-associated risk, and that animal studies were not teratogenic [12].

Wikipedia lists common side effects in adults as back and joint pain, indigestion, sleep disorders, dizziness, tonsillitis, swelling of the arms or lower legs, vomiting, adrenal insufficiency, hypertension, raised creatine phosphokinase, weight gain and anaemia [16]. It lists as contraindications active malignancy, any stage of diabetic eye disease, acute critical illness and acute respiratory failure, the last two reflecting a higher death rate seen with GH in critically ill people without GH deficiency [16][17].

In the clinical trials, safety was described as consistent with daily growth hormone, and in adults no antibodies against somapacitan or GH were detected [1][20]. Long-term registries in children and adults are enrolling to track neoplasms and diabetes over time [13][14].

Children. A phase 1 dose-escalation trial in 32 prepubertal GH-treated children with GH deficiency assessed safety and pharmacokinetics of single weekly doses against daily GH [5]. The phase 2 REAL 3 trial randomised 59 children to somapacitan or daily GH, with 3-year and 4-year results published [4][6][9]. The phase 3 REAL 4 trial randomised 200 treatment-naive children across 86 sites in 20 countries 2:1 to somapacitan or daily GH (Norditropin). Estimated height velocity at week 52 was 11.2 cm per year on somapacitan and 11.7 cm per year on daily GH, meeting the non-inferiority criterion; height SDS, bone age and IGF-I changes were similar [1]. A 3-year REAL 4 report followed [23]. A phase 3 trial in children born small for gestational age has also been published, and the REAL 9 trial is examining children with SGA, Turner syndrome, Noonan syndrome and idiopathic short stature [22][24].

Indirect comparison. Because long-acting GHs have not been compared head to head, a network meta-analysis compared somapacitan with somatrogon and lonapegsomatropin using daily GH as the common comparator, and found no differences at 52 weeks in height velocity, height velocity SDS or height SDS [18]. A review of the class concluded that weekly products gave non-inferior height velocity and similar safety to daily GH [7].

Adults. In REAL 1, a phase 3 trial of 301 treatment-naive adults randomised to weekly somapacitan, daily GH or placebo, somapacitan reduced truncal fat percentage over 34 weeks by an estimated 1.53 percentage points more than placebo (P = 0.009) [2]. A 26-week safety trial and a trial in previously treated adults compared it with daily GH and reported similar safety and efficacy, with treatment satisfaction favouring the weekly regimen [3][8][20].
Ongoing. Long-term safety follow-up studies are registered for children and adults, and a post-marketing surveillance study in adults is registered [13][14][29].

Regulatory status. The FDA approved somapacitan in August 2020 as the first once-weekly GH therapy for adults with deficiency; the EU approved it in March 2021 after a positive CHMP opinion in January of that year [16][17]. Pediatric indications were added later, and the long-acting class also includes lonapegsomatropin (Skytrofa), approved by the FDA in August 2021 as the first once-weekly treatment for pediatric GH deficiency, and somatrogon [7][17]. It is prescription-only in the US, Canada and Australia, where it is Schedule 4, and Wikipedia reports Brazil classes it under C5 (anabolic steroids) [16].

Context. Growth hormone therapy has a long history: Maurice Raben purified enough pituitary GH to treat a deficient boy in the late 1950s, roughly 7,700 US children and 27,000 worldwide received cadaver-derived GH between 1963 and 1985, and the product was withdrawn in 1985 after Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease cases, when Genentech's recombinant Protropin was introduced [17]. Idiopathic short stature became an FDA-approved indication for Humatrope in 2003, and Wikipedia describes it as one of the most controversial GH indications because specialists disagree on its definition; it reports that parents then sought GH more often for typically developing children [17]. Two 2003 NEJM editorials criticised off-label GH use and 'HGH-releasing' supplement advertising, noting no evidence of safety or efficacy for healthy adults [17]. Interest in GH for height and body composition is a recurring topic in appearance-focused communities.

In looksmaxxing communities. The only discussion found is a looksmax.org thread in which a user asks whether somapacitan is good and where pediatric growth hormone products might be obtained, without a substantive answer [11].

timeline.event: Recombinant growth hormone replaces cadaveric pituitary GH after Creutzfeldt-Jakob cases [17].
FDA approves daily GH (Humatrope) for idiopathic short stature [17].
First human dose trial of somapacitan in healthy subjects starts [15].
Phase 1 dose-escalation trial in prepubertal children with GH deficiency is published [5].
REAL 1 adult and REAL 3 child phase 2 results published; FDA approves Sogroya for adults with GH deficiency in August [2][4][16].
European Union approval in March; FDA approves weekly lonapegsomatropin in August [16][17].

claims.claim: One shot a week is as good as daily GH

claims.believers: Adults on GH replacement report leaner bodies and more energy.
claims.experts: In REAL 1, somapacitan reduced truncal fat percentage by an estimated 1.53 points more than placebo over 34 weeks in adults with deficiency.[2][20]

claims.claim: GH products are safe for healthy people seeking height or muscle

card.summary: A weekly albumin-binding growth hormone for diagnosed GH deficiency and some short-stature conditions; no data for height otherwise.
card.note: Prescription drug; trials in diagnosed conditions only.

quick.overview:
Somapacitan (Sogroya) is a once-weekly growth hormone injection. In the US it is labelled for growth hormone deficiency in children and adults and for several pediatric short-stature conditions.

Trials compared it with daily growth hormone in diagnosed patients. No study has tested it for height or appearance in people without a diagnosis.
quick.mechanism: It is a growth hormone derivative that binds albumin reversibly, extending its action, and binds the GH receptor with effects partly mediated by IGF-1.
quick.risks: The label lists warnings including neoplasm risk, glucose intolerance, intracranial hypertension, fluid retention, hypoadrenalism, hypothyroidism and hypersensitivity. It is prescription-only.

chain: Weekly injection replaces daily growth hormone in diagnosed deficiency
Sustained GH/IGF-1 signalling supports growth while growth plates are open
Greater height velocity in children with growth conditions
angle.text: In children with diagnosed growth hormone deficiency or related short-stature conditions, somapacitan supports growth in height in the same way daily GH does, with fewer injections. In adults with deficiency it has been shown to reduce truncal fat and improve body composition. Published trials were run in diagnosed patients; none tested it for height or looks in people without a diagnosis.
